children.text: The Clinton administration appointed William Daley, brother of Chicago Mayor Richard Daley, as NAFTA czar to lead the push for congressional approval of the free trade agreement after labor and environmental side accords were finalized. In California, a coalition of Latino/a organizations pushed back against what they described as a surge of anti-immigrant scapegoating. Within a single day, U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno, two U.S. senators, Governor Pete Wilson, and the state legislature all introduced measures targeting undocumented immigrants. MALDEF Vice President Arturo Vargas drew a historical parallel to earlier periods when immigrants became targets during economic downturns, including the Depression and the 1950s. Businessman Ed Vasquez of the Latino Business Association pointed out that Latino/a-owned businesses in Los Angeles alone generated $6.5 billion in annual revenue, refuting the claim that immigrants were a drain on the economy. In New York City, polls showed Republican candidate Rudolph Giuliani leading Mayor David Dinkins 54 to 41 percent among Latino/a voters ahead of the fall mayoral election, with Latino support seen as pivotal to either candidate's prospects. A report from the Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities noted that Latino students were enrolling in higher education in growing numbers, but that institutions were not adequately preparing for the anticipated increase.
The Pedro Albizu Campos Statue Controversy

The Chicago Park District voted to reject the donation of a bronze statue of Puerto Rican nationalist Pedro Albizu Campos, who had led Puerto Rico's only armed revolt against the United States and was convicted of conspiracy to overthrow the government. Supporters rallied outside the park district headquarters and presented a petition with 3,000 signatures. Alderman Billy Ocasio accused the board of applying a double standard it had never used for other donated statues, including monuments to Confederate general Robert E. Lee. Opponents, including city Human Services Commissioner Daniel Alvarez, argued that Campos relied too heavily on violence as a political tool and was an inappropriate role model. Supporters countered that the community, which ranked among the most economically disadvantaged Latino/a groups in the country according to the 1990 census, needed symbols of valor and pride. Backers vowed to take the issue to court.

Following the conclusion of labor and environmental side accord negotiations, Maria Hinojosa hosted a reporters' roundtable with NPR's Richard Gonzalez, Mexican daily El Universal correspondent Jose Carreno, and Latino USA Washington correspondent Patricia Guadalupe. The panelists agreed that the side agreements set up enforcement mechanisms for existing laws rather than raising standards, and that their effectiveness remained untested. Gonzalez noted that NAFTA's impact on Latinos in the United States would vary sharply by geography and occupation, with border entrepreneurs likely to benefit while industrial workers in the Midwest and Northeast faced job losses. All three agreed that without the proposed North American Development Bank in a form satisfactory to the Latino Consensus coalition, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus remained deeply divided, and a successful vote was not guaranteed. A floor vote was expected no earlier than November.

East Los Angeles artist Robert Lopez, who performs as El Vez the Mexican Elvis, joined Maria Hinojosa to discuss his act. Lopez described how a stint curating an Elvis exhibition at a Los Angeles folk art gallery inspired him to travel to Memphis and perform an Elvis-inspired set in front of Graceland, rewriting the songs to reflect the Mexican-American experience. He rechristened Blue Suede Shoes as Huaraches Azul, and That's Alright Mama as Esta Bien Mamacita. Lopez framed the act as a reclamation of the American Dream, arguing that the story of a poor man rising to the top of the entertainment world belonged not just to white Americans but to immigrants, Latino/as, and people of all backgrounds. Lopez was in negotiations for a TV sitcom and preparing for his first Las Vegas appearance.
Young Latino/as at World Youth Day

Producer Betto Arcos gathered voices from among the 150,000 young people who attended Pope John Paul II's visit to Denver for World Youth Day. Latino/a youth expressed a range of views on education, political representation, Clinton's presidency, gays in the military, and abortion. Opinions on abortion were notably divided, with some supporting women's right to choose and others opposing it on religious grounds. Several speakers called for stronger investment in Latino/a education and greater Latino/a political power.
